Peter. Originally a Galilean fisherman named Simon or Simeon, he was called to be Jesus's first apostle alongside his brother Andrew. Jesus renamed him Cephas, which is Aramaic for "rock," or its Greek equivalent Peter. Jesus declared "upon this rock I will build my church," and he gave Peter the keys to the kingdom of heaven along with the authority to bind and loose on earth—language interpreted by Christians as foundational ecclesiastical authority.

At Jesus's trial, Peter denied knowing Jesus three times during a single night, fulfilling Jesus's prediction that he would betray him before the cock crowed. Yet he was one of the first apostles to witness the post-Resurrection appearances of Jesus. His restoration is described in John 21, where Jesus asks him three times "Do you love me?"—inverting the three denials with three affirmations.

After the Resurrection, Peter emerged as the acknowledged leader of the apostles and the Jerusalem church. He presided over the apostolic council and made key decisions about the inclusion of Gentiles. In the Acts of the Apostles, he performs the first public miracle, healing a beggar, and he is imprisoned and flogged for preaching Jesus's resurrection. He served as the chief missionary to Jewish communities, while Paul became the apostle to the Gentiles.

Peter authored the epistles 1 Peter and 2 Peter, addressing Christian suffering and faithfulness in the face of Roman persecution. Early Church tradition places his death in Rome under Nero, executed by crucifixion—reportedly upside-down at his own request, unworthy of dying as Jesus did. Catholic tradition venerates him as the first Pope, making him the foundation of papal authority and apostolic succession.

Peter's journey from impulsive fisherman to rock of the church exemplifies a central Christian narrative of transformation through faith and divine grace. His denial and restoration prefigure the church's wrestling with human weakness and redemption. The Gospels portray him as lovably flawed—quick to speak, slow to understand, yet fundamentally loyal. The early Acts shows him as a pragmatic leader wrestling with theological questions. His letters, read against the backdrop of his own persecution, carry an authenticity of experience; he writes to the persecuted from his own suffering. He stands as the guarantor of apostolic authority, the link between the historical Jesus and the institutional church, and the prototype of the converted sinner.
